subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Why the photoelectric effect shows that light comes in particles
Threshold frequency: the lowest frequency that releases electrons
Einstein's equation: work function, maximum kinetic energy and stopping potential
How electron diffraction shows that matter behaves as a wave
Matter shows both wave and particle behaviour
Calculating a particle's de Broglie wavelength from its momentum
Compton scattering as further evidence that light is made of particles
Why a scattered photon comes out with a longer wavelength
Calculating the Compton shift from the scattering angle

questions.q: Which observation from photoelectric experiments cannot be explained by the classical wave theory of light?
options: Photoelectrons are emitted without any measurable delay, even in very dim light.
More photoelectrons are emitted each second when the light is made much more intense.
More photoelectrons are emitted each second when the frequency of the light is raised.
Every photoelectron leaves the metal with kinetic energy exactly hf − Φ.
optionWhy: In the wave theory, energy spreads over the wavefront, so in dim light an electron would need time to absorb enough energy to escape. Experiment shows emission begins at once, because a single photon delivers all the energy one electron needs.

A student who counts every photon-model result as evidence against waves picks this. The wave theory also predicts it: more intense light delivers more energy per second and so releases more electrons per second. It does not distinguish the two models.

A student who thinks frequency controls the number of electrons picks this. It is not one of the features of the effect: the number of photoelectrons per second is proportional to the number of photons arriving per second, which is set by the intensity, and at a fixed intensity a higher frequency means fewer photons per second, not more. Frequency sets the maximum kinetic energy, E_max = hf − Φ.

A student who reads Einstein's equation as applying to every electron picks this. It is not observed: photoelectrons have a range of kinetic energies up to a maximum, E_max = hf − Φ, because electrons from below the surface lose extra energy on the way out.
questions.explain: In the wave theory, energy spreads over the wavefront, so in dim light an electron would need time to absorb enough energy to escape. Experiment shows emission begins at once, because a single photon delivers all the energy one electron needs.

questions.q: Which statement defines the threshold frequency of a metal?
options: The maximum frequency of light that can release photoelectrons from the metal
The frequency of light that releases the most photoelectrons per second from the metal
The frequency below which photoelectrons leave the metal only after a long delay
The lowest frequency of light that can release photoelectrons from the metal
optionWhy: A student who thinks lower-frequency, longer-wavelength light carries more energy picks this. Photon energy E = hf rises with frequency, so there is a MINIMUM frequency for emission. The threshold WAVELENGTH is the maximum wavelength.

A student who thinks frequency controls the number of photoelectrons picks this. The number emitted per second is set by the intensity (photons per second). The threshold frequency is simply the lowest frequency at which any emission happens.

A student who thinks electrons can build up energy from the light over time picks this. Below the threshold frequency no photoelectrons are emitted at all, however long the light shines, because one photon cannot supply the work function and energy does not accumulate.
Below the threshold frequency f₀, each photon has less energy than the work function (hf < Φ), so no electron can be released, whatever the intensity. At f₀, hf₀ = Φ.
questions.explain: Below the threshold frequency f₀, each photon has less energy than the work function (hf < Φ), so no electron can be released, whatever the intensity. At f₀, hf₀ = Φ.

questions.q: Ultraviolet radiation of wavelength 200 nm falls on a clean zinc plate. The work function of zinc is 4.30 eV. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the stopping potential for the photoelectrons?
optionWhy: A student who gives the whole photon energy to the electron uses E_max = hf = 6.22 eV. At least the work function, 4.30 eV, is needed to free the electron, so E_max = 6.22 − 4.30 = 1.92 eV and V_s = 1.92 V.

A student who thinks the stopping potential measures the work function writes eV_s = Φ. The stopping potential stops electrons that have already escaped; it measures their maximum kinetic energy, eV_s = hf − Φ = 1.92 eV.
A student who adds the work function uses E_max = hf + Φ = 6.22 + 4.30 = 10.5 eV. The electron must use energy Φ to escape, so it is subtracted: E_max = 1.92 eV.

questions.q: Monochromatic light falls on the emitting plate of a photocell. The potential of the collecting electrode relative to the emitting plate is varied. The photocurrent is zero at −1.2 V and below; it rises as the potential increases and levels off at 3.0 μA above about +2 V. The intensity of the light is then doubled, with its frequency unchanged. Which describes the new current–potential graph?
options: The current is zero at −1.2 V and below, as before, and levels off at 6.0 μA.
It becomes zero only at a more negative potential, and levels off at 6.0 μA.
It becomes zero only at a more negative potential, and still levels off at 3.0 μA.
The current is zero at −1.2 V and below, and still levels off at 3.0 μA, set by the potential.
optionWhy: Doubling the intensity at the same frequency doubles the number of photons, and so of photoelectrons, per second: the saturation current doubles to 6.0 μA. Each photon still has energy hf, so E_max and the stopping potential are unchanged.

A student who thinks brighter light gives electrons more energy picks this. The saturation current does double, but the energy of each photon, hf, is unchanged, so E_max = hf − Φ and the stopping potential of 1.2 V stay the same.

A student who swaps the roles of intensity and frequency picks this, making intensity control the energy and not the number of electrons. It is the reverse: intensity sets the number per second, doubling the saturation current, and frequency sets E_max.

A student who applies Ohm's law to the photocell thinks the potential alone sets the current. The saturation current is the charge of all the photoelectrons emitted per second, which doubles when the number of photons per second doubles.
questions.explain: Doubling the intensity at the same frequency doubles the number of photons, and so of photoelectrons, per second: the saturation current doubles to 6.0 μA. Each photon still has energy hf, so E_max and the stopping potential are unchanged.
questions.working: At a fixed frequency each photon has the same energy hf, so E_max = hf − Φ is unchanged and the stopping potential is still 1.2 V (the current is zero at −1.2 V). Doubling the intensity doubles the number of photons, and so of photoelectrons, per second: saturation current = 2 × 3.0 μA = 6.0 μA.

questions.q: In an electron diffraction tube, electrons accelerated through a potential difference of a few kilovolts pass through a thin film of graphite and strike a fluorescent screen, where bright concentric rings are seen. How does this experiment provide evidence for the wave nature of matter?
options: The rings form where electrons bounce off the carbon atoms like balls, at particular angles.
The rings are a diffraction pattern, at angles that fit a wavelength λ = h/p for the electrons.
Electrons in the beam interfere with one another beyond the film, and the rings mark where they reinforce.
The rings form because each electron follows a wavy path between the rows of atoms.
optionWhy: A student who treats electrons purely as particles picks this. Particle collisions with atoms would scatter electrons over a spread of angles, not into sharp rings whose size depends on the electrons' momentum as λ = h/p predicts.

Diffraction is a wave property. The rings are at angles where waves scattered by the regularly spaced carbon atoms reinforce, and those angles match the de Broglie wavelength h/p. Changing the electrons' momentum changes the ring sizes as this wavelength predicts.
A student who thinks electrons must meet to interfere picks this. The same pattern builds up even when electrons pass through one at a time; each electron's own wave is diffracted by the atoms.

A student who pictures an electron moving along a wave-shaped path picks this. The electron's wave is not a trajectory; it describes where the electron is likely to be detected, and diffraction of that wave produces the rings.
questions.explain: Diffraction is a wave property. The rings are at angles where waves scattered by the regularly spaced carbon atoms reinforce, and those angles match the de Broglie wavelength h/p. Changing the electrons' momentum changes the ring sizes as this wavelength predicts.

questions.q: Electrons are sent towards a double slit at such a low rate that only one electron is in the apparatus at any time. Each electron is recorded as a single dot on a detector screen. At first the dots seem to be scattered at random, but after many thousands of electrons they form a pattern of bright and dark fringes. What do these results show about each electron?
options: It is deflected by the electrons that went through before it, and this builds up the fringes over time.
It is detected at one point, like a particle, but wave interference sets where it is likely to land.
It follows a wavy path from the slits, which carries it to one of the bright fringes.
It spreads out over the whole screen as a wave, and each dot marks the place where most of it arrived.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the pattern needs electrons to interact with one another picks this. Only one electron is in the apparatus at a time, and the pattern does not depend on the rate; each electron interferes only with its own wave.

Each detection is a single dot, which is particle behaviour. Yet the dots build up an interference pattern even though the electrons pass one at a time, so each electron's own wave, passing both slits, sets the probability of where it lands. This is wave–particle duality.

A student who pictures the wave as a wavy trajectory picks this. There is no such path; the wave determines only the probability of detection at each point, and the dots land at random positions within that distribution.
A student who treats the electron as a spread-out classical wave picks this. Each dot is a whole electron, with all its charge and mass, detected at one point; nothing of it arrives anywhere else.
questions.explain: Each detection is a single dot, which is particle behaviour. Yet the dots build up an interference pattern even though the electrons pass one at a time, so each electron's own wave, passing both slits, sets the probability of where it lands. This is wave–particle duality.

questions.q: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 2.0 kV. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, m_e = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and treat the electron as non-relativistic. What is the de Broglie wavelength of the electron?
optionWhy: A student who uses the photon relation λ = hc/E gets (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸)/(3.20 × 10⁻¹⁶) = 6.2 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. That holds only for photons; for an electron λ = h/p with p = √(2m_eE_k).
A student who uses p = √(m_eE_k), leaving out the factor 2, gets 3.9 × 10⁻¹¹ m. From E_k = p²/2m, p = √(2m_eE_k), giving λ = 2.7 × 10⁻¹¹ m.
A student who uses E_k = 2000 (the energy in eV) as if it were in joules gets p = √(2 × 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × 2000) and λ = 1.1 × 10⁻²⁰ m. The kinetic energy is 2000 eV = 3.20 × 10⁻¹⁶ J.

questions.q: An electron and a proton have the same kinetic energy, and both move at speeds much less than c. The mass of the proton is about 1830 times the mass of the electron. How do their de Broglie wavelengths compare?
options: The proton's wavelength is about 43 times as long as the electron's.
The electron's wavelength is about 1830 times the proton's.
The electron's wavelength is about 43 times the proton's.
They have equal wavelengths, as the particles have equal energies.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a heavier particle has a longer wavelength inverts the ratio. At equal kinetic energy the proton has the larger momentum, √(2m_pE_k), so it has the SHORTER wavelength.

A student who assumes equal kinetic energy means equal speed uses λ = h/mv with the same v and gets the mass ratio. The lighter electron moves faster, so its momentum is only √1830 ≈ 43 times smaller.
λ = h/p = h/√(2mE_k). At equal E_k, λ ∝ 1/√m, so λ_e/λ_p = √(m_p/m_e) = √1830 ≈ 43.
A student who uses the photon relation λ = hc/E for particles thinks equal energies give equal wavelengths. For particles with mass, λ = h/√(2mE_k), which depends on mass as well as energy.
questions.explain: λ = h/p = h/√(2mE_k). At equal E_k, λ ∝ 1/√m, so λ_e/λ_p = √(m_p/m_e) = √1830 ≈ 43.
questions.working: λ = h/p and p = √(2mE_k). With equal E_k: λ_e/λ_p = √(2m_pE_k)/√(2m_eE_k) = √(m_p/m_e) = √1830 = 42.8 ≈ 43.

questions.q: In Compton's experiment, X-rays of a single known wavelength were scattered by electrons in a block of graphite, and the wavelengths of the scattered X-rays were measured at several angles. Which result is evidence for the particle nature of light?
options: The scattered X-rays included a longer wavelength, shifted by an amount that increased with angle.
The scattered X-rays all had the same wavelength as the incident X-rays, at every angle.
X-rays were scattered in all directions, as balls would be when they hit a target.
The scattered X-rays included a longer wavelength, shifted in proportion to the incident wavelength.
optionWhy: Classical wave theory predicts scattered radiation of unchanged wavelength. The shifted wavelength, increasing with angle as Δλ = (h/m_ec)(1 − cos θ), is exactly what a collision between a photon of momentum h/λ and an electron predicts.

A student who pictures a photon bouncing off an electron like a ball off a wall expects no change. This was not observed, and an unchanged wavelength is what the classical WAVE model predicts, so it could not be evidence for photons.

A student who takes any particle-like description as evidence picks this. Waves are also scattered in all directions by electrons, so scattering alone does not distinguish the models. The evidence is the angle-dependent increase in wavelength.
A student who expects the shift to be a fixed fraction of the wavelength picks this. The Compton shift depends only on the scattering angle, Δλ = (h/m_ec)(1 − cos θ), not on the incident wavelength.
questions.explain: Classical wave theory predicts scattered radiation of unchanged wavelength. The shifted wavelength, increasing with angle as Δλ = (h/m_ec)(1 − cos θ), is exactly what a collision between a photon of momentum h/λ and an electron predicts.

questions.q: When an X-ray photon is scattered by a free electron, the scattered photon has a longer wavelength than the incident photon. What is the reason?
options: The photon loses some of its speed in the collision, which stretches its wavelength.
The photon transfers some of its energy to the recoiling electron, so its energy hc/λ decreases.
Some photons are absorbed, so the scattered beam is weaker and has a longer wavelength.
The photon gains energy from the electron, and a photon with more energy has a longer wavelength.
optionWhy: A student who treats a photon like a material particle whose energy depends on speed picks this. A photon always travels at c in a vacuum; its energy falls by a decrease in frequency, which means an increase in wavelength.

Energy and momentum are conserved in the collision. The electron recoils with kinetic energy taken from the photon, so the scattered photon has less energy E = hc/λ, and therefore a longer wavelength.

A student who confuses the intensity of a beam with the energy of each photon picks this. Each scattered photon's wavelength is longer because that photon lost energy to an electron; the number of photons has no effect on the wavelength.
A student who thinks longer wavelength means more energy picks this. E = hc/λ: a longer wavelength means LESS energy. The photon loses energy to the electron, which is initially at rest.
questions.explain: Energy and momentum are conserved in the collision. The electron recoils with kinetic energy taken from the photon, so the scattered photon has less energy E = hc/λ, and therefore a longer wavelength.

questions.q: Photons are Compton scattered by free electrons. For which scattering angle θ is the increase in the wavelength of the photons greatest?
options: θ = 90°, where the photon turns at right angles
θ = 0°, where the photon carries straight on
θ = 180°, where the photon is scattered straight back
No single angle: the shift is h/m_ec at every angle
optionWhy: A student who thinks a right-angle deflection is the largest change picks this. At 90°, 1 − cos θ = 1, so Δλ = h/m_ec; at 180°, 1 − cos θ = 2, twice as large.
A student who uses cos θ in place of (1 − cos θ) picks this, since cos θ is greatest at 0°. A photon that is not deflected is not changed: 1 − cos 0° = 0, so the shift is zero.

Δλ = (h/m_ec)(1 − cos θ) is greatest when cos θ = −1, at θ = 180°, where Δλ = 2h/m_ec = 4.85 × 10⁻¹² m. A photon that rebounds straight back has the largest change of momentum and gives the most energy to the electron.
A student who takes the constant h/m_ec to be the shift itself picks this. The shift is (h/m_ec)(1 − cos θ), which rises from zero at 0° to 2h/m_ec at 180°.
questions.explain: Δλ = (h/m_ec)(1 − cos θ) is greatest when cos θ = −1, at θ = 180°, where Δλ = 2h/m_ec = 4.85 × 10⁻¹² m. A photon that rebounds straight back has the largest change of momentum and gives the most energy to the electron.
questions.working: Δλ = (h/m_ec)(1 − cos θ). 1 − cos θ ranges from 0 (θ = 0°) through 1 (θ = 90°) to 2 (θ = 180°), so the shift is greatest at θ = 180°: Δλ_max = 2h/m_ec = 2 × 2.43 × 10⁻¹² m = 4.85 × 10⁻¹² m.
